2. The petitioners, the landlords of the suit premises, instituted Other Suit No. 172 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif aforesaid against the tenant, Sukhendu Bikash Das, father of the opposite-parties Nos. 1-4 and husband of opposite party No.5, for his eviction from the suit premises on the allegations that the tenant defaulted in payment of rent and the landlord required the premises for bona fide use and occupation. Sukhandu contested the suit denying the allegations made in the plaint by filing written statement. The trial court decreed the suit for eviction and for recovery of Tk. 190/- as compensation by its decree dated 30.11.78. The defendant's appeal being Other Appeal No. 31 of 1979 against that decree was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong. Against the decree of the Subordinate Judge the Rule obtained by the defendant Sukhendu Bikash in Civil Revision No. 274 of 1983 was also discharged on hearing by an order of this Court on the 2nd January, 1985. After the discharge of the Rule by the High Court Division the petitioners put the decree in execution in the Other Execution Case No. 23 of 1984. 

 4. The learned Munsif, however, dismissed the Execution Case holding that the right of tenancy in respect of the suit premises was a. personal right and not heritable on the death of the judgment-debtor. Being of the view he also vacated the order of substitution and observed that the decree became infructuous on the death of the tenant, the petitioners were to institute a fresh suit against the opposite-parties herein for their eviction from the suit premises. The learned Munsif relied upon the case of Abdus Sattar & others Vs. Suresh Chandra Das & ors., 32 D.L.R. (A.D) 170; Abdul Latif and another Vs. Abdul Mannaf and others, (1982) 2 B.C.R.(A.D) 428 and Md. Abdus Salam Chowdhury Vs. Jamini Ranjan Das and ors. in Civil Revision No. 756 of 1981 decided on 6th May, 1982, a photostat copy of a certified copy of the judgment in Civil Revision No. 756 of 1981 was placed before me by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties. 

 5. The learned Advocate for the petitioners very strenuously argued that he decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 170 although held that the tenancy at will creates a personal relation between the original landlord and the tenant and is terminable by death of either party yet in the present case the Execution Case against the opposite party Nos. 1-5 will not be defeated merely on the ground of death of the judgdebtor during. Pendency of the case as the point mint which requires consideration by this Court in the instant case was not mooted and decided in the aforesaid decision. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman further argued that a executing Court cannot go beyond the decree and in this case as the decree was put into execution by. The tenant during his life time, the executing Court should not have entertained the application for dismissal of the Execution Case. 

 6. Mr.Jvloqbul Ahmed on the other hand submitted. relying on the decisions referred to above that on the death of Sukhendu Bikash Das the tenancy was determined as the same was in the nature of personal right and not heritable and as such the opposite parties are not bound by the decree and the execution case is liable. to be dismissed against his clients and it was rightly dismissed by the trial court. 

 7. Now let us revert to the question: Whether a decree obtained by a landlord against his tenant and put into execution by him is executable or not against his heirs on his death during the pendency of the execution case? To answer this question it would be necessary first to examine certain provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Premises Rent Control Ordinance before we enter into the discussion of the decisions referred to above: Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman placed before me section 2(11) and section 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control OrdiNance, 1963. According to the definition as given in section 2(11) of the Code a legal representative means a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person and includes any person who inter- meddles with the estate of the deceased. Section 50 of the Code provides that where a judgment- debtor dies before the decree has been fully satisfied, the holder of the decree may apply to the Court which passed it to execute the same against the legal representative of the deceased. Section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 that tenant means any person by whom, or on whose account rent it payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 and a person continuing in possession afar the determination of a tenancy in his favour. It appears from the definition of tenant as given in section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 that the expression "Tenant" includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code. The present opposite parties being heirs of Sukhendu Bikash Das are, in my opinion, his legal representatives within the meaning of section 2(11) C.P.C. as they represent the estate of their predecessor-in-interest, Sukhendu Bikash Das. Now let us consider some of the decisions on this point. In the case of Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee and others Vs. Haracharan Singh, 1934 Lah. Addision, J. in delivering the judgment of the Division Bench has observed as follows :- 

 9. In view of the definition of legal representative as given in section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and on the strength of the judicial pronouncements made in 1934 Lah 1 and 1934 All 474 I am led to hold that definition of legal representative as contemplated in section 2(11) of the Civil Procedure Code shall be given a wide meaning to include the heirs of a deceased tenant who died during the pendency of an Execution Case started in pursuance of a decree for eviction of the tenant from, the suit premises for the limited purpose for execution of the decree obtained against the legal representatives of the-tenant, This matter may be viewed from another angle. The opposite-parties are in possession of the suit premises since. The time of their predecessor-in-interest, Sukhendu Bikash Das, on the basis of the lease created in his favour. But on his death the opus  rites are continuing in possession the premises in suit but not on the basis of any lease. But even then their possession can not be said to be a possession of trespassers and such possession of the opposite parties herein, in my opinion, would not be unconscionable toehold as possession of the tenants by sufferance. This view taken by me gets support from the following observation made in 32 DLR (AD) 170. 

 10. As in this case the decree was put into execution against the defendant and on his death as the opposite parties who are in possession of the premises in question, the Execution Case is legally enforceable against them as they are tenants by sufferance. In the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Mohiuddin & ors. 38 DLR (AD) 97 it has been held that the heirs of the deceased tenant who continue to stay in the premises arc held to be tenants by holding over and were under legal obligation to restore possession to the landlord. Now let us consider the decision reported in (1982) 2 B.C.R (AD) 428. In (1982) BCR (AD) 428 it has been held that as tenancy cease to exist on the tenant's death the heirs of the decease; tenant do not inherit the tenancy and as such they arc not entitled to restitution. The principle of law lair down in this case can hardly be disputed. The facts of this case are different from the facts of theistic case and the question which is posed before me is al together different from the one considered in that case. The decision of that case rests on the question of restitution of the premises to, the legal heirs on termination of tenancy on the death of the tenant. II view of the facts and the question that fell for deter monition in that case being all together different from the present one the decision has no direct bear of in the instant case before us. 

 12. Mr Shafiqur Rahman further argued that an executing Court cannot go beyond the decree and in the case as the decree was passed against the tenant Sukhendu Bikash Das during his life time and the decree not being a nullity the executing Court wrongly entertained the application under section 151 of the Code for dismissal of the Execution Case arid dismissed the same illegally. He referred the case of Baliram Hari Vs. Mukinda Kisan, 1951 Nagpur 145 wherein it has been held that executing Court cannot question a decree and it is its duty to execute the decree as it is and not to go beyond it. The principle of law in this respect is well-settled. But in view of the question that falls for our determination we are not called upon to decide this issue in this case before us. 

 13. The trial Judge also fell into error in dismissing the execution case invoking inherent jurisdiction under section 151 C.P.C. inasmuch as for dismissing the execution case as on the ground the decree being nullity and infructuous on the death of the tenant an independent suit lies and thus there being an alternative remedy provided for in the Code itself the exercise of power under section 151 C.P.C. on the part of the learned Munsif in dismissing the execution case is unwarranted in law.
